speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RELIEF COMMITTEE BY CANADIAN RED CROSS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement I would like to make to the house with respect to the disastrous floods in Europe, and I make it because I am sure all hon. members and all those they represent are actively interested in what is taking place and in what is being done in that respect.
I dispatched this morning to the Hon. Leopold Macaulay, chairman of the central council of the Canadian Red Cross at 95 Wellesley Street East, Toronto, the following telegram:
Pursuant to telephone conversation with national commissioner and in accordance with the suggestion which I made in House of Commons on February 3, I am now formally requesting the Canadian Red Cross Society to assist in the establishment of a national European flood relief committee and to act as the administrative arm of the committee.
It is further suggested that any funds contributed for relief purposes be given to the committee and that the Red Cross would act for it in providing transportation and distributing relief supplies through the league of Red Cross Societies (Geneva) and the National Red Cross Societies of Great Britain, the Netherlands and Belgium.
Louis S. St. Laurent
At the suggestion of the national commissioner I sent to each of the provincial premiers the following message:
My dear Premier:
I have today sent the following telegram to the chairman of the central council of the Canadian Red Cross Society.
Then follows the text of the telegram which I have just read and which I will not repeat at this time. After the quotation I added the following:
I have been asked by the society to inquire if you would be willing to serve on the committee which it is proposed to establish.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RELIEF COMMITTEE BY CANADIAN RED CROSS
speechtext:
To deal with the points raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in the order in which he raised them, Mr. Speaker, I would mention first the information he has
given us about the plans being made to facilitate the transmission of assistance from Canada to Great Britain, Holland and Belgium. I feel sure there will be general agreement that the Canadian Red Cross Society is extremely well fitted in every way to assume the responsibility which it is accepting in this case. Happily, that organization continues its activities in peace as in war. Sometimes we are inclined to forget the great services it does perform in times of peace. The regular blood donor services and other activities of that kind have been continuing without interruption throughout the years, so there will be already in existence in every community across Canada local branches of the Red Cross Society which will be able to carry out this work.
As each day goes by, in fact as each hour goes by, the extent of the tragedy becomes more apparent. It is sometimes by a single incident that the nature of the general tragedy may be better understood. I think many hon. members will have had something of the nature of a personal feeling of tragedy when they read today that a mother and children, who had gone back to Holland from Georgetown to visit her parents, had been drowned in the flood.
In the three countries affected the record of the tragedy mounts, and most certainly the members of this house on both sides will welcome the steps that are being taken to make it possible for Canadians to give tangible expression to the deep emotion that has been aroused by these events.

subtopic: RELIEF COMMITTEE BY CANADIAN RED CROSS

It is
hardly necessary for me to say that we in this group are particularly glad that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is taking quick steps to mobilize the sympathies of the people of this country in connection with the relief of those who are suffering from this great catastrophe in Europe. In talking to people I find that many would like to contribute individually. In view of what the Prime Minister has said, I believe the arrangements being made will give them an opportunity of doing that. I believe it is a fine thing that it can be done at this time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ERECTION OF MONUMENT ON PARLIAMENT HILL

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ERECTION OF MONUMENT ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a meeting of the
cabinet this morning a decision was reached to place in the supplementary estimates to be recommended to parliament for the fiscal year 1953-54 an item to provide for the erection on parliament hill of an appropriate monument in memory of the late Sir Robert Borden.
All hon. members know that 1954 will be the 100th anniversary of Sir Robert Borden's birth, and it was felt that it would be appropriate to recommend commemoration of that centenary by the erection of a permanent memorial to one who was recognized by all Canadians, without any distinction of party affiliation, as one of our great prime ministers. No Canadian who knows anything about the history of the last half century of our country ignores the great part that Sir Robert played during the first great war, and the great part that he always played in the constitutional development of this Canadian nation. It is a fair assumption to make, I think, that every hon. member of the house will be glad to approve of that recommendation. I believe the people of the country as a whole will also be happy if this monument can be unveiled at the time of the centenary celebration of Sir Robert's birth.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ERECTION OF MONUMENT ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Naturally I join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and with other members of the house in expressing gratification that steps are being taken to commemorate in the form of a statue the memory of a very great Canadian.
It is only natural that the members of the Conservative party should have a feeling
[Mr. Low.)

of particular pride in regard to this great man; but as the words of the Prime Minister have clearly indicated, this is not a matter of the pride of one party or of the people of any part of Canada, but rather an expression on behalf of all the people of Canada in tribute to a man who played a great part in the development of our country. He assumed responsibilities during the first world war that extended beyond the ordinary responsibilities of a man in that high office. All of us will recall that it was his insistence at the meeting of those who gathered at Versailles that first asserted in definite form Canada's position by his demand that Canada sign, as a sovereign nation, the treaty of peace which formally terminated the first world war.
Statues of this kind are not merely for the purpose of giving satisfaction to those who have some personal recollection of the man himself, or for the satisfaction to his relatives. It is a good thing for every country that there be before the minds of our people, and particularly the young people, evidence of the fact that under our democratic system of state, a great contribution is made to the advancement of the state by those of different parties who share a common affection for the country in which we live.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ERECTION OF MONUMENT ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Coming
from Nova Scotia as I do, it is a special satisfaction to hear the announcement of the Prime Minister that a monument is to be erected to a great Canadian and a great Nova Scotian, Sir Robert Borden. I do not want to detract from his position in any way, but coming from the county of Cumberland in Nova Scotia I should like to point out that another great Nova Scotian, who up to now has had no monument erected to him, is worthy of note. He was prime minister of Canada also. There would have been no Canada as it is today; there would have been no west; there would have been no Canadian Pacific Railway; there would have been no industrial development at a time when there was that industrial development in Canada, were it not for Sir Charles Tupper. I should like to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister the suggestion that a monument to Sir Charles Tupper has been too long delayed. While I am happy to hear that a monument is to be erected now to that great Nova Scotian, Sir Robert Borden, I ask the government to give consideration to the erection of a monument to that other great Nova Scotian and Canadian.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ERECTION OF MONUMENT ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
The
Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has referred

to the erection of a memorial to the late Sir Robert Borden. This decision of the cabinet will probably receive more unanimous support than cabinet decisions ordinarily receive. I probably had not changed my political affiliation in the early days of Sir Robert Borden's political activities, but even if I have changed them since that time I can still say that he was a great Canadian and made a great contribution to the development of Canada as a nation. If I may be allowed to mention it, I have recently been reading a memorial to another great Canadian. I am referring to the book by Donald Creighton on Sir John A. Macdonald. It really made me feel proud that I had, not in an intimate way but merely as a young lad, known of this very great Canadian. I believe commendation is due Mr. Creighton, not just for the biography he has written but because in my opinion he has written, for the first time, Canadian history that is really readable and interesting.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ERECTION OF MONUMENT ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
With
respect to the announcement in connection with the monument to Sir Robert Borden, I think it is a nice gesture that the Liberal party of Canada has made in deciding to have a monument erected. We certainly support the suggestion and we shall be anxious to see the project completed. Perhaps some of us might attend the unveiling of the monument.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ERECTION OF MONUMENT ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a humble member from Nova Scotia I want to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the government on what they are doing toward putting a statue on parliament hill in commemoration of one of the greatest men this country has ever had, and one of our greatest prime ministers. I had the pleasure and, I should say, the honour of reading law in the office of Sir Robert Borden in Halifax. I did not see too much of him at the time but I think he was the kindliest man I ever met in my life.
Some time ago I said a word about Sir Robert Borden in connection with a matter which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) brought before the house today, namely the signing of the treaty of Versailles. The matter of placing monuments on parliament hill in commemoration of our great men is something worthy of our Canadian people. It is something to indicate that after all we have here a united nation irrespective of politics or anything else.
The story of Sir Robert Borden is one well worth reading. I often think that the government of this country, whether it be
Committee on Standing Orders Conservative or Liberal-and I presume that is the only kind we shall ever have-should get somebody to write, in accurate and historic form, the history of the great men who have ruled over the destinies of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a word or two with respect to this motion. I believe that it asks the house to approve a recommendation of the committee on standing orders that certain requirements be dispensed with so far as a particular bill is concerned which it is proposed to introduce.
As hon. members of the house are aware, the bill referred to in this report is with respect to a considerable sum of money that was left over from the contributions that were made at the time of the flood in Manitoba in 1950. I believe the amount of money is of the order of $1,450,000 and that the petitioners in this case are asking from parliament a bill to authorize the setting up of a Canadian disaster relief fund.
I need not go into the details as to how this money came to be left over, but I think it would be appropriate to suggest at this time that those who are behind this petition and this bill might give consideration to the possibility of finding some way to turn that money over to the fund which has been announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) today, so that it might be used immediately for relief work in the United Kingdom, in the Netherlands and in Belgium.
The thought that this might be done has already been suggested in an editorial in one of the Winnipeg newspapers, and I have no doubt that the other one will probably express the same viewpoint. I am sure all those in Manitoba will support that view. It seems rather strange that we should think of holding on to a large sum of money if it is needed at all at the present time. As was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) the other day, we in Manitoba are deeply conscious of the way in which people around the world came to our assistance when we were in need in 1950. I think it would meet with the wishes and

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RELEASING BUTTER
speechtext:
should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Will the minister make a statement to the house as to whether it is the intention of the government to release government-held butter to the trade in the very near future?
Will the minister also comment on the statement made by his parliamentary assistant in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) as to the reason for placing restrictions on the sale of this butter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO GOVERNMENT POLICY IN RELEASING BUTTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was kind enough to give me a copy of his question. I think I can best answer it by reminding the house that over the last four years we have been following the same general policy, namely that of stabilizing the price to farmers throughout the summer months, and we have been making an attempt also to stabilize the price to consumers throughout the winter months. The first winter we were not so successful in stabilizing the price to the consumers. I am not going to comment any further than to say that. During the second winter we had some difficulties as well. During the last year we have been getting along fairly well with that policy.
During the past summer we took delivery of the butter of farmers at all times when it was found impossible or impracticable for others to pay as much as 58 cents a pound for it. We bought the butter at 58 cents, or at comparable rates across Canada, to an extent which gave us about 40 million pounds of butter by the 1st of November last. At about that time we announced to the public of Canada that a reasonable return for the butter which the government had, in order to cover our costs, would be 62 cents a pound. We therefore said on December 4 last that any time we delivered butter until May 1, 1953, we would deliver it at 62 cents, which placed everyone in the trade in a position to know that there was at that time 40 million pounds of butter which could be delivered to them at 62 cents and when occasion arose to make delivery necessary, we would act so as to keep ourselves in position to carry out our undertakings.
Between then and now we have delivered 10 million pounds. The trade has 15 million pounds, and there is coming on to the market month by month 10 million pounds


that we cannot get control of in any way. Those 10 million pounds go to the trade. In other words, for the month of February there are 25 million pounds of butter available in Canada to the trade, and that much butter will not be consumed in Canada in the month of February. All of that butter will be available.
The only objective we have in mind is to see to it that our undertaking that we would be able to deliver butter to the trade right down to May 1 next at 62 cents a pound will be carried out. We will be delivering butter to the trade in order to take care of the situation and in such a manner as to provide that we carry out to the consumers the undertaking we gave that butter would be available to them at a price based on a wholesale price of 62 cents right through to the end of this present dairy year, which is down to the end of April.
On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) addressed a question to the Prime Minister on that part of President Eisenhower's address to congress on the state of the union which concerned Formosa. In replying at that time the Prime Minister indicated that more information, might be available later in the week when it was hoped that a discussion on external affairs would take place. That discussion cannot, I think, now take place until next week, and I would therefore like to give information supplementary to that which was given by the Prime Minister on Monday.
I have had an opportunity, as have hon, members, since Monday of studying the text of the statement by the President of the United States to which I have referred. In that statement, as hon. members know, the President announced the modification of the presidential order to the seventh fleet issued by his predecessor on June 27, 1950. That order, which was given, as the house will recall, shortly after the aggressive attack on South Korea, was in the nature of an instruction to the United States seventh fleet both to prevent any attack upon Formosa from the mainland, and also to ensure that Formosa should not be used as a base of operations against the Chinese communist mainland.
The order was issued, of course, before the large-scale intervention by Chinese communist forces in Korea, and its objective was

to neutralize Formosa in order to limit the hostilities arising out of the aggression of June 25, 1950, on the Korean peninsula.
As the Prime Minister indicated Monday, the original order was an action taken on the sole responsibility of the United States government, just as the recent action modifying it with respect to what the President has termed the employment of the seventh fleet to "shield communist China" was taken on the sole responsibility of the United States government. That, however, does not make the matter one of little or merely indirect interest to other countries, including Canada.
With respect to the position of the Canadian government, while we remain resolved to carry out our United Nations obligations in Korea, we do not think that the defence of Formosa, which has not been assumed by the United Nations, should be confused with the defence of Korea, which has. As I have mentioned on several occasions in the house, on May 15, 1951, on May 22, 1951, and on April 1, 1952, our consistent position has been that this island should be neutralized, so far as that is possible, while hostilities continue in Korea. Our view has been that the final disposition of Formosa should be a subject to be discussed at a conference on Far Eastern problems which should be held when the fighting ceases in Korea; and we strongly supported the statement of principles approved by the political committee of the fifth United Nations general assembly which specifically provided for such a conference. In any decision regarding the future of Formosa, the wishes of the people there would naturally be a primary consideration.
In considering the possible effects of this recent action by the United States government, I should emphasize that on Far Eastern issues, as on other questions in which we are both concerned, the fundamental and long-term aims of Canada and the United States are similar, although naturally we may differ on occasions in our approach to specific issues and as to how these long-term aims can best be achieved.
Canadians of course know President Eisenhower well. They feel a deep gratitude for the services he has already rendered the free world and have full confidence, I am sure, in his peaceful and constructive purposes. And I am convinced that one of these purposes-as it is the purpose of this government and this parliament and our country, and the purpose of the other governments who are now engaged in Korea-is to end and not to extend the Korean war.
It should also be noted that in his statement President Eisenhower stated clearly
Inquiries of the Ministry that "this order implies no aggressive intent on our part". Nor should we, I think, assume that because of this order any large scale operations in the near future are likely to be undertaken by Chinese nationalist forces on the mainland. The order does, however, rescind that part of the original order by which' the United States seventh fleet would prevent any such operations.
The original order did give, I suppose, to the communist forces in China a feeling of immunity from attack from Formosa. This has become increasingly unacceptable to the people of the United States, as the Chinese communists have continued their aggression in Korea and only recently rejected a resolution, approved by the present United Nations general assembly, which could have ended the war there on acceptable terms. The United States government has, therefore, found it necessary to take action to alter a situation which was considered no longer to have its original justification.
It is no doubt hoped that this change may keep more Chinese communist forces in China and hence have an advantageous effect on United Nations operations in Korea. It would of course be another matter, as hon. members will be aware, if Chinese nationalist raiders or invading forces were escorted or protected in their operations by the armed forces of other United Nations governments. We have no reason to believe, however, on the basis of any information available to us that any such development will take place, the consequences of which would be far-reaching.
We are not of course committed by, though naturally we are concerned with, the action taken in Washington in connection with this matter. The government will follow developments with the closest possible attention and take appropriate action to make our views known if and when the occasion so warrants. Meanwhile I think it would be unwise and premature to jump to dogmatic or critical conclusions concerning the step taken by the United States government, and announced in a statement by President Eisenhower which contained so much that was wise and heartening to us all.

May I ask a supplementary question. First, can the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell the house when a debate on this subject will be undertaken; and second, whether the government was informed of this contemplated action on the part of the United States, and whether the government has been informed of any other action, in addition to this, in the same area?

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: So far as the first question is concerned, it is hoped that a discussion on external affairs may take place in the early part of next week, perhaps Monday or Tuesday. Replying to the second question, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) indicated last Monday, we were informed as a matter of courtesy about this United States unilateral action before it took place. We were informed on Friday last that this paragraph would be included in the President's message. We have no information about any possibility or likelihood of any subsequent action being taken by the United States government.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ACQUISITION BY CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
speechtext:
I have no objection to speaking now.
The Saint John Bridge and Railway Extension Company was incorporated by the statutes of New Brunswick (1881) 44 Victoria, chapter 44, with authority to construct and maintain a line connecting the Saint John and Maine Railway at Fairville, New Brunswick, with that of the Intercolonial Railway at its terminus in Saint John, New Brunswick. It was also authorized to construct a bridge across the Saint John river as part of this undertaking. The company was declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada by chapter 26 of the statutes of Canada, 1883.
By the act last mentioned the federal government was authorized to make a loan to the Saint John Bridge and Railway

Extension Company of $433,900 upon the security of a mortgage on the entire assets and property of the company. The loan was made and the mortgage given by the company to the federal government on December 10, 1883.
The loan was repayable in 15 years and in 1898 under authority of chapter 9 of the statutes of 1898, the maturity date was estended for another 15 years. No further extension has been given but interest has been paid annually at 4 per cent.
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company acquired a majority of the common stock of the bridge company in 1905 and for many years has owned all outstanding shares and securities. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has advised the government that it is now prepared to repay this loan and wishes to take an assignment of the mortgage. The Canadian Pacific represents that it is necessary, upon repayment, that all title of Her Majesty in the properties mortgaged become vested in the Canadian Pacific and that its right to ownership of the shares and securities be beyond question.
Although the bridge company is a separate corporation, it is by ownership and operation an integral part of the Canadian Pacific system. In view of this it is desirable that the companies be given the powers contemplated by sections 151 to 153 of the Railway Act.
This is the ordinary type of bill which is passed under similar circumstances when a debt or loan is repaid. It consists of the usual assignment, not only of the mortgage security on the property but also the right to sue on the demand covenant as well as the rights under the usual covenants mentioned in the document.
This is a simple bill for the purpose of enabling the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to repay the loan to the government and to have the title of Her Majesty in the properties covered by the mortgage vested in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

subtopic: SAINT JOHN BRIDGE AND RAILWAY EXTENSION COMPANY

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not rising to oppose this bill as I know it has been considered by another place, but I think perhaps there is a little more interest in it than might be indicated by what the minister has said. I do not intend to go into the history of the Saint John Bridge and Railway Extension Company except to say that in the early days this bridge provided an important link in our Canadian transportation system between the eastern part of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and the western part of the province and the United States.
Saint John Bridge Company
When this matter first came up I read over the debates in 1883 when this particular bill asking for a charter from the province of New Brunswick to a private company was before the dominion house. The resolution was presented by Sir Leonard Tilley, who was the member for the city of Saint John. It was pointed out at that time how important this railway link was. Sir Edward Blake, who took part in the debate, as did Sir Charles Tupper, objected to a private company getting control of such an important link in our transportation system.
The objection at that time was based on the fact that there were other railways which were interested, and that there was a possibility of the shares of the company being purchased by one railway to the disadvantage of the others. The shares were purchased, as the minister has told us, by the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1905, but there has been no intimation that this has worked to the disadvantage of any other company. Sir Edward Blake referred also to the matter of tolls which he contended should be controlled by the federal government if they did not build the . bridge themselves. Sir Leonard Tilley explained that they would be under the control of the federal government.
I think it is only natural that the Canadian Pacific should get control of this bridge and railway. As far as is known I believe they have acted fairly with the other railways. This bridge is used not only by the Canadian Pacific but also by the Canadian National and in the past it has been used by other railroads. Now that the Canadian Pacific virtually will be the owners of this bridge I should like to ask the minister what arrangements have been made for the protection of the Canadian National and other railways which will use it. Is this bridge to be a separate entity or are running rights to be given, not only over the bridge but over that part of the railroad line which is owned by the Canadian Pacific and used by the Canadian National?
There is another point that occurs to me. This act was passed by the federal house 70 years ago, and it is over 70 years since the act was passed by the New Brunswick legislature. In Saint John for the past number of years there has been a feeling that there should be a bridge across the Saint John harbour. I should like to ask the minister whether any representations have been made to his department for assistance in the construction of a bridge across that harbour, which possibly might be joined in by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
These are some questions which I should like to have the minister answer. I would

Saint John Bridge Company suggest also that the bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) for introducing into the discussion of this bill a subject which has been uppermost in the minds of all of us in Saint John for some time. This railway bridge is the only bridge across the Saint John river or harbour between Saint John and Fredericton. Along with the highway bridge which is adjacent, it is the only link between Saint John proper and Lancaster and thence the southwestern section of the province.
The question of a new bridge has been under study by the people of Saint John for many years. The need for civil defence has brought this problem more prominently to the fore. I suggest to the minister that he give some thought to the question of a bridge across Saint John harbour. We must remember that practically the only means of transportation now existing between the central and western sections of the city of Saint John and the city of Lancaster which lies adjacent thereto is an antiquated ferryboat, the operation of which is costing the city of Saint John a considerable amount of money each year, because it operates at a deficit.
I know that before very long stronger representations than ever are going to be made to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) in connection with this proposed bridge. I hope that by having this advance notice of the intention of the people of Saint John he will be in a position, and the engineers of his department will also be in a position, to give the question full consideration. Perhaps the engineers might work on the subject and see if there is not some way whereby the people of the city of Saint John can be given more ready access to that part of the city which lies on the western side of the harbour. It should also be taken into account that this railway bridge, together with the adjacent highway bridge, constitute the sole link between the east and west sides of the Saint John river above Fredericton.

He said: Mr. Speaker, in 1949 parliament enacted the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation Act. Under that act the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, commonly referred to as the
C.O.T.C., was established as a crown corporation without share capital. Part VIII of the Financial Administration Act contains provisions that are designed to regulate the financial operations of crown corporations.
Second, in 1952 the Income Tax Act was amended to apply to crown corporations specified in schedule D of the Financial Administration Act. The Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation is one of these crown corporations which is now subject to the Income Tax Act.
The bill provides for the removal of the mandatory requirement on the corporation to pay annually to the Receiver General an amount equal to its operating profit, and also the provision requiring payment to the corporation of an amount equal to its operating loss, to be paid from moneys appropriated by parliament for that purpose.

subsubtopic: RECOVERY OF INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS
speechtext:
Before attempting to explain the present bill it should perhaps be observed that under section 7 of the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act shipowners are permitted each year to transfer to reserve account a limited sum of tax-free money. The purpose of that section is to enable an owner to accumulate sufficient funds to meet certain extraordinary expenses which he has to incur periodically in connection with the special surveys or inspections of his ship. The intervals at which special surveys must be held are either every four or every five years depending upon whether the survey is for purposes of insurance under the rules of a classification society or for purposes of safety under the Canada Shipping Act.
It has been found necessary to amend the section in order to guard against the loss of revenue by leaving tax-free reserves in the hands of shipowners for indefinite periods of time. Accordingly the present amendment 68108-105J
Vessel Construction Assistance Act provides machinery for periodically recapturing or rendering taxable such of these reserves as are not or cannot be used for the purpose for which they were intended as, for instance, in cases where the amounts set aside exceed the costs of survey or where a ship is lost or sold at some time during one of these four or five year cycles.
The amendment now before the committee requires all reserves to be brought into profit and loss account in the year in which the survey was completed or in which the ship was lost or sold. It should be observed that under the amendment the reserve account periodically becomes self-liquidating. If, on the one hand, the ship is lost or sold, the reserve must thereupon be brought into profit and loss account. If, on the other hand, nothing happens to the ship and the survey is held in due course, the reserve is brought into profit and loss account in the form of a credit and the costs of survey are entered in the same account by way of offsetting debit.

subsubtopic: RECOVERY OF INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act was passed in 1949 with the object, among others, of encouraging shipbuilding in Canada. It contained a provision for accelerated depreciation in the case of the construction of new vessels and also in the case of repairs, as I read the original act. Then there was this help given in the way of allowing a reserve to be set up from which the quadrennial survey and certain other expenses which would occur from time to time could be provided for in the intervening years.
This amendment before the committee today purports to make provision for recovering taxation on these reserves. In effect it is certainly not going to be of any help to the shipbuilding industry. It is the reverse. It is a help to the Department of National Revenue.
I can see the reason for making these reserves taxable where the survey has not been held. For example, if the ship has been lost in the meantime, then there would appear to be no reason why that money which has been put in a reserve should not become taxable. But it is not so clear why the money which has actually been spent on the survey should be taxable.
The minister did not explain that point in his opening remarks. But as I read section 1 of the bill, once the survey has been made and has been paid for, taxation is to be levied on the amount actually used in payment for the survey. I do not understand why such payments should not be allowed
1546	HOUSE OF
Vessel Construction Assistance Act as an operating expense and thus not be taxable at all. I may not have the correct explanation of the section, but to me it reads in that way.

subsubtopic: RECOVERY OF INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS
speechtext: They are allowed as an expense.

subsubtopic: RECOVERY OF INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS
speechtext:
I hope that is correct. We can go into that matter in a little more detail in a few minutes.
While one object of the original act was to aid shipbuilding in Canada, another equally important objective was to modernize the Canadian merchant navy. This had become necessary because of the fact that the ships we built during the war were all slow cargo vessels quite unable to compete with the faster ships which were being built by other countries, commencing immediately after the war.
I have here the various reports of our own Canadian maritime commission, all of which substantiate my statement that Canada needed a modern, fast merchant navy. Similar statements have been made from time to time by the minister himself. I doubt whether he or anyone else would question the fact that one of the great needs in Canada since the end of the last war has been to build up a modern merchant navy. If we cannot succeed in doing that it is only a matter of time until we cease to be a maritime nation in so far as deep-sea shipping is concerned.
This plan was therefore brought in to encourage the building of modern cargo vessels. There was also, of course, what was known as the replacement plan under which, if the owner of one of the slow, war-built cargo vessels sold his ship, he had to put the proceeds into an escrow fund managed by the Canadian maritime commission, the idea being that that money would eventually be used in the construction of a modern vessel.
The result of these two plans-the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act and the replacement plan-has been that Canada has built a great many ships for the great lakes trade and also for coastal shipping. For that reason I believe that the plans can be considered as being at least partially successful. Mind you, the bulk of our shipbuilding now is naval shipbuilding. I do not know the percentage-the minister can tell us that-but perhaps 75 or 80 per cent of the value of shipbuilding in the country today is for the Department of National Defence or for some other department of government.
As to naval shipbuilding and building for the great lakes trade and for the coastal


trade, the situation seems to be fairly satisfactory. But when we turn to the building of vessels for the deep-sea trade, the picture is entirely different. We have built very very few modern cargo vessels. I believe that two tankers are now being built, but so far as I am able to ascertain from the fifth report of the Canadian maritime commission, which is dated June 30, 1952, no other modern cargo vessels or modern tankers have been built for the ocean-going trade.
If we turn to page 6 of the report we find great jubilation because of the fact that these two tankers are being built. The paragraph in question reads:
What must also be regarded as an encouraging development took place toward the end of 1951.

Why is this legislation being introduced by the Minister of Transport at all? Why is it not income tax legislation and in the Income Tax Act? One of the difficulties the minister gets into, in trying to answer the questions of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, is that it is a matter that comes under national revenue or finance.
I recall that not many years ago an attempt was made to bring the income tax legislation up to date, and put it into consolidated form, so that one could find all the references to income tax in one piece of legislation. Now, we discover that outside of the Income Tax Act is this legislation which deals with an income tax matter. I suppose the minister will say that the lawyers in the Department of Finance, the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Transport have all approved, and therefore we are supposed to approve too. It does seem to me that the idea of rationalizing our legislation has been lost, and here we

have an income tax matter that should be not under the Minister of Transport at all but in the Income Tax Act itself.

subsubtopic: RECOVERY OF INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS
speechtext: I would suggest to the minister, Mr. Chairman, that he have this section rechecked by the Department of National Revenue and by his own officials. With all respect to the minister, I am afraid that the way this section is worded the whole thing is taxed, including what has been spent for surveys. There is not such a rush about the bill that it could not be reconsidered by the department with that objection in mind. I would ask that that be done.

subsubtopic: RECOVERY OF INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS
speechtext: I can see no reason for rechecking the bill, because I gave my assurance to the house that I have gone over it carefully, and that three groups of lawyers have gone over this bill very carefully. After all, if the amendment is read in conjunction with section 7 of this act, which in turn is read in conjunction with the relevant sections of the Income Tax Act, there could only be one conclusion, and that is that the aggregate amount of the deductions in respect of the vessels that have not previously been included-that would be, I take it, the difference between those that were exempted and those that are not now exempted. It seems to me that the addition of the words "and had not been spent'' would add little or nothing. I am not objecting to the words being put in there, as they simply clarify the intention, but this bill has been given such careful consideration by these three groups that I hesitate to consent to the suggestion.

subsubtopic: RECOVERY OF INCOME TAX DEDUCTIONS

As to the other point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, may I say that we are, of course, as familiar with his suggestion as is the committee familiar generally with this bill. Annually, for some years, he has been making the suggestion that the Auditor General should be appointed the auditor for the Canadian National Railways. After study, I think it was indicated in a previous debate that it was considered that the Auditor General was probably eligible for an appointment as auditor; but it was also pointed out that one of the big advantages of having an audit made by the same firm, if satisfactory service has been rendered, is the fact that a continuous audit is being conducted.
The Canadian National Railways is an extremely intricate corporate organization. It is highly desirable that the auditor be familiar at all times with the rather complicated corporate relationships and subsidiaries of this large organization.
In past debates I think even the hon. member agreed that the expense of audit would not likely be less were the Auditor General

to be appointed. It is known to the committee that the interests of the Canadian National Railways are international and that portions of the audit must take place not only in the United States but in the United Kingdom and in France, as a result of the audit of Trans-Canada Air Lines. The particular firm which has been appointed by parliament in other years and is proposed now has international branches.
Another reason for appointing the same firm of auditors is that railway accounting is frequently subject to special legislative direction as, say, in the United States, as to the form of accounting that is done there. Hon. members know that even we in Canada have recently passed legislation under which the railways are directed to keep their accounts in a certain way. The present auditors are familiar with that legislation. In addition, there are complications as to the past bylaws of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways which govern accounting procedure. There is a requirement for familiarity with past orders in council and other legislation that applies to the accounting requirements of the railways. En masse these various things are of sufficient consequence that it is felt that a considerable break in experience and familiarity would take place if a change in the audit was made.
It has been estimated that it would take any firm of auditors several years to make an adequate acquaintance with the accounting system of the railway, and those who are familiar with it are of course in a much better position to spot quickly anything that needs attention. In past debates the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has pointed out that the Auditor General makes references to certain things in his report to parliament. I want to point out to hon. members that it is parliament that is appointing the auditors in this case. They do so annually, and under the statute the auditor is obligated to report to parliament. A senior representative of the auditors of the Canadian National Railways, and it includes the Trans-Canada Air Lines, as hon. members know, comes to parliament annually and subjects himself on behalf of the firm to examination by the members of the railways and shipping committee.
In addition to that, under the section, he is obligated, just as is the Auditor General, to point out to parliament, through this committee, anything that he thinks requires attention. And certainly, the years that I have been familiar with these reports and through my attendance at the railways and shipping committee, I cannot recall that any members of the committee ever suggested
Canadian National Railways-Auditors that there was any inadequacy in this method of appearances before a parliamentary committee and the reports that we got from the auditor when he comes to our committee.

The house resumed, from Friday, January 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Winters that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize grants of assistance to provinces for the conservation of water resources under the terms and conditions specified in the said measure, such grants not to exceed thirty-seven and one-half per cent of the projects and to be paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the above-mentioned purposes:	and to provide that all
officers, clerks and employees required for carrying out the provisions of the measure shall be appointed in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Service Act.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I make no apology for taking the time of the house to make a few comments on this resolution. I listened to the Lilliputian statement by the minister, on the introduction of the resolution, and after listening to it and later reading it I am not quite sure of the complete purpose or scope of the measure.
So far as I could judge, the government still believes in a piecemeal approach to the problem of water conservation, to such an extent that it has indicated by this measure and by the minister's remarks that the conservation and development of water resources is to be the responsibility of two separate departments of government.
Furthermore the group to which I belong is disappointed to see that this resolution is not part of a national policy dealing with the conservation of soil, forest and water resources, brought about as a result of a dominion-provincial conference and through dominion-provincial co-operation. We are not alone in this respect. Many other voices in Canada have been raised suggesting the need for an over-all national policy, and expressing some disappointment with the government's present piecemeal approach to this most important question.
In support of the argument I am making I should like to read a portion of an editorial appearing in the Country Guide for November of 1952. 1 have said before in the house that the editor of this paper is well qualified to speak and to write about this most important question. He says this:
It is, therefore, of particular interest to Canadian agriculture that a delegation of provincial ministers of agriculture met the federal minister of agriculture not long ago, to request that the principles underlying the work of P.F.R.A. be applied across Canada. The delegation is also reported to have voiced grave concern over the fact that provincial governments tend to attach far less importance to the diversion and use of the waters of rivers and streams for agricultural purposes, than to the protection of cities and towns from the danger of flooding.
The truth seems to be that in most Canadian provinces the problem of adequate soil and water conservation is too serious to be solved entirely by the provinces. We urgently need a national soil and water conservation policy. Since 1935 an excellent beginning has been made within the Palliser triangle, the area to which the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation administration has been restricted. The value of the work already done is beyond calculation, but what Canada really needs is a general purpose, rather than a special purpose, policy and program.
We in this group heartily support the ideas expressed in that editorial. I would point out that it emphasizes two things in particular, the first of which is the need for an over-all national nolicy for soil, water and forest
Water Resources
conservation and, secondly, the necessity for extending the principles of P.F.R.A. to all provinces in Canada.
I trust that even this resolution may be a step in that direction on the part of the government. I must say that those of us in this group are glad of this evidence of growing government recognition of this most serious and important problem. The introduction of this resolution without doubt does provide a basis for some measure of co-operation between and assistance to the provinces.
I listened with keen interest to what has been said by previous speakers in the debate, particularly to the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue), who is well acquainted with prairie problems, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), who frequently in the house has shown his concern over water conservation as applied to the Palliser triangle, and particularly to the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson).
I might say that while I do not agree with the hon. member for York West when he deals with the symbols of wealth-when he deals with gold-I listen with great enjoyment to his pedestrian eloquence when he speaks upon such subjects as the conservation of our natural resources and deals, shall I say, with problems concerning the conservation of real wealth.
I listened carefully to his speech and read it afterwards and in my view he made a definite contribution to the debate and to our knowledge on this subject. The facts he gave the house are worth rereading and careful study.
The policy of the C.C.F. is based upon the principles of co-operation and conservation. Year after year, session after session and speech after speech we have indicated our support for a policy which would deal with the conservation of human and natural resources. To succeed in that kind of policy there is an urgent necessity for planning.
I would draw to the minister's attention the fact that even in the introduction of this resolution the government is giving effect, perhaps in a limited degree, to policies which have been advocated by this group through the years both in the house and throughout the country. The resolution presents an opportunity for some logical development and planning as a result of dominion-provincial co-operation.
I represent a constituency which abounds in lakes, rivers and streams, a constituency with immense water resources. But even with all those resources the people I represent are very much concerned with certain problems related to the conservation and development of those water resources. They

Water Resources
are very concerned about flood control. They are very concerned at the present time about the shortage of water for power. I know that power does not come under this measure and I assure the minister that I will not get out of order. I shall leave the South Saskatchewan river dam entirely alone and I trust my remarks will be strictly in order.
They are concerned about the shortage of water suffered on occasion by certain cities, towns and small communities. They are very concerned about the erosion of the banks of various rivers by waters when in flood. They are concerned about these problems and these problems will continue to exist so long as governments fail to accept their responsibility by co-operating and planning to solve them in the very near future.
At this point I cannot resist taking advantage of the opportunity to bring to the attention of the house the fact that uncontrolled free enterprise must bear a large share of the responsibility for our defaced forests, our vanishing wildlife, our roaring floods, our dried-out ranges and the many gullied parts of this country. Uncontrolled free enterprise has carried on in Canada up to date without biophysical understanding or social responsibility. I think that is a fair statement to make of the conditions that exist at this time in this country.
Uncontrolled and greedy free enterprise has not only produced the physical conditions that exist, but in my opinion it has created a waster psychology that would have appalled our frugal forebears and which is regarded as lunacy by people in other lands who have given serious consideration to this problem for many years. When I say "waster psychology" I mean it because I think many of us in this country are most wasteful. We waste our power; we waste our water; we waste our soil; we waste our forests; we waste our tin cans; we waste our waste paper; we waste our rubber and we waste many other things.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Horses.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
Because we have no over-all policy governing the conservation of natural resources, a policy which realizes that the natural resources of this country will be depleted in time, we have that result. If we spent as much time advertising the value of conservation as we spend in advertising the dangers of B.O. the Canadian people would become conscious of the seriousness of this question.
Free enterprise and industrial society has produced a state of mind on the part of many people who live in the larger centres 
that simply fails to appreciate the basic facts of our existence. At this point I should like to quote from an interesting article by Christopher Morley in "Streamlines" as follows:
We hear about the agricultural problem of soil erosion; hillsides denuded of fertile topsoil . . . or great regions of middle western richness scoured off by dust storms. Surely not less serious is the matter of mind erosion; the dust storms of daily excitement and of continual triviality can easily blow away the sensitive topsoil of the spirit. The result is a barren and shallow nervous credulity.
I quote that because I think it indicates the state of mind that prevents people having a full appreciation of the seriousness of certain basic problems such as this one v.'hich face the Canadian people at this time. In our opinion only action by governments can repair the damage which has been done to our natural resources during the last fifty years under uncontrolled free enterprise. Therefore, I repeat that we in this group are glad that the minister has introduced this resolution and we offer our support.
The hon. member for York West has said that water shortage is a North American problem. This growing shortage of water affects nearly every community. This shortage of water is occasioned by abnormal runoff, increased industrial use, unnecessary evaporation and lack of forest coverage. These things are increasingly affecting our stores of water from year to year and because of this situation the future of many communities in Canada is threatened.
Surface water has three channels of escape-surface drainage, seepage into the ground and evaporation. I shall not deal with these because I think the hon. member for York West covered that aspect of the matter when he spoke the other evening. But I do want to direct the attention of the house to another cause of increased and abnormal run-off to which possibly some people have not given consideration.
This is due to millions of roof tops, the increasing area of paved street and highways and airports and the tremendous urge today to cover the earth with concrete and asphalt. This has created a great problem in the areas surrounding large centres of population because of the abnormal run-off. Large amounts of water are permitted to escape unnecessarily which could be utilized under an over-all policy of conservation.
The hon. member for York West referred to the lowered water tables, losses through evaporation, increased use of water for industrial purposes and the pollution of our streams. Evidence of this can be found in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I

shall not take the time to deal with this in detail, but I should like to quote an authority which does indicate the seriousness of the situation. I should like to quote from "Water Conservation Notes" for September, 1952, by J. L. Van Camp, general manager, Canadian Forestry Association, as follows:
Professors A. F. Coventry and J. R. Dymond, reporting on "Water, a National Treasure", in the book "Conservation and Nature Activities", give data on a survey which was made in King township in York county, Ontario in the mid 1930's. From that township they report that of the 200 miles of permanent streams which originally ran at all seasons of the year, this total has been reduced to less than 30 miles when the survey was made. At that time also, 17 per cent of the wells in the township went dry each summer.
A survey made in an adjacent area between Toronto and Dundas showed that 672 of all streams in an area of 13,000 square miles no longer flowed continuously. On some of them, now dry or reduced to a meagre flow in summer, the remains of mills and dams indicated that water was formerly available in sufficient quantity to provide power for grist and sawmills.
Further data showing the undesirable difference between peak flood and peak drought conditions is given for the west Humber river near Toronto. During a flood in March, 1942, when nearly an inch and a half of rain fell in 48 hours, the west Humber was carrying four thousand cubic feet a second past a given point. Almost half of the entire amount of water which fell was in lake Ontario within 12 hours. The water was opaque with sediment, and from one measurement it was shown that 2,700 tons of soil an hour was being carried into the lake.
I could go on at greater length but I think that that demonstrates the great need for an over-all consideration of this problem by federal, provincial and municipal governments.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion it is a complete fallacy that industrial civilization can continue to produce a permanently higher standard of living. None of the industrial nations have maintained high standards of living without access to adequate areas of productive land. As a matter of fact, European industry has been supported for years by food produced in America. In Canada industrial expansion is of recent date but even in that short period there is evidence that we are consuming and abusing our natural resources at an increasingly alarming rate.
At this point I would ask the minister a question and ask him to answer when he replies in closing this debate. I consider, as do the members of this group generally, that our snowfall in Canada is a billion dollar crop, and I have been interested in reading of some studies that have been made with respect to the conservation of snow. I do not know if this resolution will provide for further studies in that direction or whether
Water Resources
it will provide for giving application to certain ideas for the conservation of snow. I understand that experiments have been carried on throughout the years in the United States, and I understand by one engineer in Ottawa, which indicate that you can conserve snow and save abnormal run-off.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is a great loss of snow or water on the prairies through abnormal run-off occasioned by heat. The water, flowing over frozen surfaces, has not an opportunity to penetrate into the subsoil. Experiments have been conducted, I understand, with a view to creating an icy surface on the snow which will prevent excessive evaporation. Some experiments to date offer almost breath-taking possibilities. By spreading carbon particles on the snow in a mechanical way, either by ground vehicles or by helicopters, it is possible to produce an icy surface and tremendously reduce evaporation so that a much greater quantity of water coming from the snow goes into the soil. I would like the minister to tell the house when he speaks at the conclusion of this debate if anything has been done in that connection in his department.
I do not want to speak at too great length, Mr. Speaker, but before concluding I wish to say a few words about the administration of water conservation policies in Canada. The agricultural institute of Canada, I understand, made a submission to the government last year and at that time made reference to this legislation which was forecast in the speech from the throne. The brief presented by the agricultural institute of Canada contended that any conservation of water that affected the soil should be under the administration of the Department of Agriculture. I have read the brief very carefully, having been interested in this subject for years, and I think the point of view expressed by the agricultural institute of Canada is quite sound. I think that the administration of water resources should be in the hands of people who are close to the farmers, and close to the people who are going to use the water.
Furthermore, I find that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture supports the agricultural institute of Canada and I would like to quote briefly from a letter I received on December 12 from Mr. C. G. Groff, secretary-treasurer. This is what he had to say:
In view of the fact that there is now a bill before the house with respect to water conservation, we discussed the matter at our executive meeting just after the conference a week ago. Our attitude is that all conservation matters, having as their ultimate objective the conservation of the soil from which the food of the people is produced. should be carried out and administered

Water Resources
under the Department of Agriculture, in co-operation with the various provincial departments of agriculture. We had before us a resolution passed by the agricultural institute of Canada and our executive endorsed this resolution.
There you have the scientific body concerned with agriculture expressing an opinion and you have the organization representing the farmers themselves supporting that opinion. I find further evidence to support that opinion in the country and I wish to quote from an editorial appearing in the November issue of the Country Guide entitled "Sensible Conservation Policy". This is what the editorial has to say:
The ministers might well have gone much further in their representations. They could well have urged that in any national or provincial program involving soil and water conservation and development, the responsibility for administration should rest in departments of agriculture, both provincial and federal. We already have too many examples of divided responsibility within provincial governments, including the governments of Manitoba and Alberta, which have led to inefficiency and lack of progress. If we are not to lose valuable time, and money which we cannot afford to squander, it is imperative that all senior governments in this country agree on one important administrative principle. The principle is that whenever conservation policies are applied, either to land or water for the benefit of agriculture, such policies and programs should be planned, administered and developed, by those who are trained and employed to serve agriculture. Too many millions of dollars have been lost, in this and other countries, for us to entrust these primary responsibilities to engineers, indispensable as they are. Similarly, central administrative officers, in departments other than agriculture, are too far away from the soil and its needs, and from the farmer and his problems, to fully realize that these are the really basic factors involved.
The experienced agricultural administrator, agronomist, soil scientist, agricultural economist, and agricultural engineer, as well as the nonagricultural engineer, are each essential to a well-planned and effectively developed program. Surely, simple logic demands that the men and departments designated to carry the heaviest responsibility for the execution of any policy involving agricultural land, or water for such land, should be those specializing in agricultural matters.
Mr. Speaker, I most wholeheartedly support those contentions and those representations. In my opinion, if this legislation is to be effective it must be accompanied by co-operative research and it is imperative that research be extended from the natural sciences to the social sciences; for, if a conservation program of any type is to succeed, they are inseparable. Again, quite as necessary as research is education. To cope with research problems on a national basis we require the education of tens of thousands of Canadians and tens of thousands of Canadian children. However, in my opinion, research and education are futile unless they result in an action program that sinks well within the grass roots of our democracy, and
[Mr. Herrldge.l
with this program should be associated a program to stop waste of all types in Canada in every field of human activity. If it is to be successful, Mr. Speaker, implementation of this resolution requires that there be co-operative action between Canadians and all levels of government.
We certainly have got to plan if we are going to conserve our great water resources in Canada -by good forest management, grass cover, check dams, and other methods to prevent excess run-off, loss of water and flood damage. Our economy is dependent on water to furnish cheap transportation, heat, power, light, agriculture, forestry, water for our homes, for health and for recreation. There is no question but that it is the duty of this parliament to see that ample and good supplies of water are provided in Canada for this generation and generations to come.
In conclusion I wish to say that we in this group support the principle and the purpose of this measure and will do our best to co-operate with the government in giving it satisfactory effect.

speechtext:
It is not my intention to take much time of the house this afternoon but I do wish to take a short while to commend the government for bringing forth this resolution to assist in the conservation of water resources. When the minister spoke first on this measure, he mentioned the Shand dam on the Grand river, which happens to be just north of the riding which I represent. He also mentioned construction of the Luther marsh dam, which is also in the Grand river conservation project. I am very glad that he announced a decision had been made by this government to assist in the construction of the Glen Allan dam on the Conestogo river. I want to commend him for it. The Shand dam was started in 1939, and between 1939 and 1950 there was very little done in the way of helping to control the floods in this area. Having lived beside the Grand river, I am alive to the dangers of the Grand river when it is in flood. The Shand dam was not sufficient to control the flood waters of the Grand, and hence the Luther marsh dam was built. It is now found that that is not sufficient and the Conestogo or Glen Allan dam is being built.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think we should first try to decide the difference between flood control and water conservation. Dams will control flooding, but more than dams are necessary for water conservation. It would seem that there is, then, a duplication of services here between the Department of

Resources and Development and the Department of Agriculture. We have now a number of expert engineers employed in the Department of Agriculture under the P.F.R.A. It seems to me that the services of these expert engineers could be used to help out on this flood control work.
Water conservation should be carried out under the Department of Agriculture. I see nothing in this resolution that would show there was anything actually to be done with regard to water conservation. I should like to qupte from the resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize grants of assistance to provinces for the conservation of water resources under the terms and conditions specified in the said measure, such grants not to exceed thirty-seven and one-half per cent of the projects and to be paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament for the above-mentioned purposes; and to provide that all officers, clerks and employees required for carrying out the provisions of the measure shall be appointed in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
There is no mention there, Mr. Speaker, of co-operation with the provinces in connection with water conservation. In his speech the minister referred to the bill as an authority providing a legislative basis for federal assistance for water conservation projects of a major character across Canada. It would appear, therefore, that the measure which this resolution precedes is a measure more for the control of floods than it is for water conservation. We had hoped it would include some manner of co-operation with provincial governments to go further than just the control of floods.

I am glad to hear the
minister say that. As I said before, there is nothing in the resolution that would lead one to believe that it does. As the minister said, it is related to major projects across Canada.
I have tried to practise conservation during the number of years I have been on the farm. Water conservation would call for small dams, probably one on each farm. Conservation of the soil means the cultivation of the soil in a manner to control wastage. It requires reforestation of some slopes to control run-off. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) just mentioned conserving the snow. Well, Mr. Speaker, I know of no better way of conserving snow than planting trees to hold the snow.
As I stated at the outset, I do not intend to take long at this stage. I do want to point out that we must differentiate between flood control and water conservation. I feel that the water conservation part could be
