subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
I am
sure that the members on all sides of the house, Mr. Speaker, join in supporting the minister in moving forward this resolution. As has been pointed out, the resolution is to authorize grants to assist in the conservation of water resources. I believe we all agree that is something that has been long overdue. In many of the provinces, particularly the province of Ontario, several surveys have been made on rivers. The Ganaraska survey has been completed, and steps have been taken to conserve the water and stop the rapid run-off. A survey of the Moira river in the county of Hastings, in my constituency, has been completed and the Moira valley authority has been set up. This authority has jurisdiction over a section of the Moira river that takes in 1,060 square miles of territory.
This Moira valley conservation authority has been very active. Under their jurisdiction a $40,000 dam has been completed at Deloro for the purpose of holding back an amount of water for conservation, and also to stop flooding. I believe the hon. member who just spoke, if he reflected for a moment, would agree that the purpose of a dam is twofold. First, it is for conservation, and second, for flood control. I believe these two purposes go hand in hand. The Moira valley conservation authority has encouraged the construction of what may be termed farm ponds. These have been found quite advantageous, and though a pond may sound like a small body of water, a number of them spread through the length and breadth of a township or a county would account for many millions of gallons of water. The Moira valley authority has issued a circular containing instructions on farm ponds, the method of building them and the vital necessity for them.
Now, as I say, I am sure all members join in supporting this resolution, because without a doubt water is the greatest asset that we have in this bountiful dominion of ours. Water is so common that we sometimes forget the value of it. It is extremely cheap. Actually it is cheaper than dirt. You can purchase water which you obtain by turning on a tap in your residence, for as little as a nickel a ton, sometimes. Those hon. members who have found it necessary to buy soil, particularly topsoil, know that you have to pay up to $10 for dirt.

Water Resources
It is only when we have a shortage that we who seem to have an abundance consider the necessity for preserving and conserving water. It will be recalled that, a year or so ago, New York had a water shortage; and there they went to the extreme of asking the male citizens of the great city of New York to shave only once a day or to forget shaving one day in the week in order to try to conserve water.
Water is continuing to be more and more in demand for the purpose of producing electrical energy. I think the minister has in mind the necessity for the preservation of this great asset of ours, particularly for electrical purposes, when he brings forward this resolution. As has been pointed out, we do not yet know just what is in the bill; but I am sure that what is there will be of great benefit to Canada, as is all the legislation that the minister of this particular department brings to parliament.
By drying up marshes and lakes we have destroyed the homes and breeding grounds of useful waterfowl and fur bearers. Being charged with the responsibility of protecting our resources including fur-bearing animals, I am sure that the minister has this point in mind also when he brings forward this bill for the conservation of water.
It seems that one of the reasons why our water is not benefiting the land in the way it should is that, over the years, we have seen fit to harvest the crop of forest products without any concern as to holding back the water or as to the way in which trees act to conserve in the land the water that should be there. Consequently we have a rapid run-off; and this rapid run-off takes with it the valuable two inches of topsoil and deposits it in the rivers and in the lakes.
We in Canada are well endowed with water resources. We have the great lakes and inland lakes. We have 228,307 square miles of fresh water within our boundaries. Lake Superior forms part of our southern border; it is the largest body of fresh water in the world. We know that we have great rivers; and of these, of course, we should take proper care. We have the Mackenzie, our longest river, which stretches for 2,514 miles from Great Slave lake to the Arctic ocean. We have the St. Lawrence river and the great lakes which provide a shipping waterway 2,338 miles in length from the strait of Belle Isle to the head of lake Superior. Our sea coast is one of the longest of any country in the world, with 14,820 miles of mainland sea frontage and 34,650 miles of island frontage.
One might think that this resource would be sufficient to minister to all our human

needs. There is no doubt that it is and will be sufficient for the great population we hope to have here in a few years. But it will only be so if we take proper conservation measures such as those which I am sure the minister is going to propose in his bill.
I just rose, Mr. Speaker, for these few moments in order to commend the minister and to assure him that I believe he has the active support of all the members in the house.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
make no apologies for entering this debate at this time because this measure is one of extreme importance to us all. The time that is taken up to discuss the measure in the house will be well spent, and we shall get from it valuable information which will be of interest to us all.
When we heard the speech from the throne read by His Excellency the Governor General we were pleased to note that the government intended to bring before the house a measure to provide for conservation of water resources. We were doubly pleased when the minister introduced the resolution stating:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize grants of assistance to provinces for the conservation of water resources-
On January 30 the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) moved that the house go into committee to discuss the terms of the resolution. We regret that we cannot expand the resolution to include soil conservation, because it is very important to our national life, and particularly as soil and forest conservation are so closely allied to and associated with water conservation in this country.
As the minister pointed out in his opening remarks, the federal government did participate with the province of Ontario in a project of this kind on the Grand river and the Shand dam which was mentioned by the hon. member for Brant-Went worth (Mr. Charlton) this afternoon. In participating with the provinces on this project the federal government worked in close co-operation with the municipalities and this undertaking contributed a great deal toward lessening the danger of flood conditions that had been gradually developing to an increasing extent in that area year by year.

The government also received some valuable information from the experiments carried on there, information which will be of great value to them as this plan progresses. We were happy that this plan was broadened to include further drainage work on the Luther marsh project in the same drainage area, and now the dam on the Conestogo river, which is a tributary of the Grand. That is the third step that will assist materially in overcoming the menace that constantly threatens each spring the life and property of that very densely populated area of southern Ontario. That area is very valuable from an agricultural point of view as well. We in that section all realize the value that has come from this experiment that has been carried on as a co-operative effort in that section of Canada.
The importance of this resolution was brought forcibly to the attention of the house by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson), who spoke in this debate on Friday evening last, as reported at page 1512 of Hansard. I should like to read a brief quotation from the hon. member's remarks. He said:
For instance, the production of a ton of rolled steel requires the consumption of 110,000 gallons of water. The production of a ton of rayon yarn takes 250,000 to 400,000 gallons of water; a barrel of aviation gasoline takes from 1,050 gallons of water, if made from the natural product, to as much as 15,000 gallons of water if made synthetically.
Further on he says:
Our North American cities use approximately between 150 gallons and 160 gallons per capita per day.
The hon. member for York West is an engineer, and we all know that he is looking at it from the practical point of view. We would all derive great benefit from reading the entire speech that he made at that time.
I feel that this bill is a step in the right direction. I hope it is the beginning of a much wider policy that will embrace soil and forest conservation as well. There is increasing evidence of late that the provinces of this country are beginning to recognize the need for a greatly enlarged conservation project on a national basis. In this regard I was very glad to hear the minister say that it must be undertaken primarily through the provinces with the federal government working in the role of co-ordinating agency with the provinces in their assistance by contributions from the federal treasury. This effort calls for close co-operation and sound planning between the provinces and the Department of Resources and Development. The general and over-all picture from the federal point of view must be closely harmonized
Water Resources
with the immediate needs of the various provinces. In this manner we can possibly work out a system by which we can carefully guard those resources which we must pass on to those who are yet unborn, and who in their turn we trust will be true guardians of these great assets that we possess.
Following the first world war there was an attempt made by government agencies to adopt practices similar to what we are discussing today. However, their recommendations were presented and no action was taken. They made a really valuable study and research at that time. But during the last twenty-five years we find that all progressive countries are increasingly concerned about the rapid growth of population which tends to exploit the resources we have, and in many cases unwisely. Our great neighbour to the south, which I think has about one-half of the industrial production of the world, is beginning to be seriously disturbed about the rapidity with which their underground waters are lessening to an incredible degree. European nations for many years past have recognized the wasting assets that nature has provided, and Canada with her yet undeveloped areas is in a much more important position when it comes to legislation of this kind, because of those undeveloped resources. There is a great need for conserving them, and we as a young nation should do it.
Many books have been written, many speeches have been made, many newspaper articles and editorials have been published -and I hope many more will be published- along this very line, so that we should be able to get our people more concerned about the growing need of this important work.
Since the formation of the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations these policies have been brought closely to the attention of the people of the civilized world by the emphasis placed on the close relationship that exists between conservation, water management and our economic well-being. The unfortunate part is that we have not been able to translate these factors into effective action whereby nations will work together in the interests of all the people. We in this country unfortunately have not as yet been able to work in close enough co-operation with the provinces on this matter. I think the time is coming, and I trust it will, when we can overlook these petty differences that we have in the interests of the common good of our resources in this country. Fifty years ago Canada had approximately 5 million people. Today we have over 14 million people, an increase of

Water Resources
something like 300 per cent in our population, but our potential productivity has remained the same as it was at that time.
Someone has said that there is a lot of ruin in a nation. I think that is very true of our natural resources. Our forest and water conservation methods must be closely interwoven. The simple fact remains that while science and mechanization have increased our industrial production and agricultural production, nevertheless these gains have been made, we must agree, at the expense of lessening our water supply. The responsibility for this situation is largely due to our individual effort, but I feel that action in this regard must definitely be taken by our governments. It is a matter of great interest to us that some time ago the provincial ministers of agriculture met with our federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to discuss some of these problems. They faced the grave concern at that time that the governments of the various provinces were more inclined to attach a greater significance to the dangers of flood conditions to the towns and villages, than to make a careful study of the basic problems and define the difficulties at the source, as well as make a careful study of matters which would give protection at the source of the water supply.
It is quite possible that a large-scale plan of reforestation and a system of diversion of our rivers and streams, similar to projects that have been undertaken by P.F.R.A., could be carried out very effectively in this regard.
In that part of the country in which I have lived in recent years, we have been given ample proof of the devastating results which can be achieved when rampaging waters are uncontrolled. We have in that area a very capable conservation commission, to which reference was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton). Then, too, if the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Macdonald) were permitted to speak in the house on this measure 1 believe he would say that the conservation commission has done a very excellent job in the capacity in which it has been working.
Nevertheless their tasks are definitely made more difficult because of the fact that they do not have the financial assistance that would permit them to carry out an extensive conservation plan in that area, such as they would have liked to achieve. As a result of the valuable experience we have had in that section, I would have no hesitation in supporting the policy the minister is now advocating. I would approve any policy which would give similar results to every section in Canada.
It is a matter of great importance however that the administration of this should very definitely remain primarily with the provinces, working in close conjunction with the federal Department of Resources and Development. Then, further, it should also be a policy which would embrace soil, water and forest conservation. No one of these projects can be worked effectively if it is operated separately, because it is necessary that all three be embraced to have an effective conservation program.
It is essential that the handling of this project should be done definitely in co-operation with the provinces, under the direct jurisdiction of capable experts in agricultural matters, as well as capable engineers who understand conservation projects. These should include men who are well skilled in this work both from the federal and provincial points of view.
These suggestions may lay a framework for what would at least be a beginning of something that will need continuous and close study for all time. This is only the beginning. If we are to meet the challenge which faces us increasingly from year to year, we must proceed from this point. Speaking from an agricultural point of view, Canada has today better than three-quarters of a million families engaged in agriculture. These families have a great stake in this country in the form of land and equipment. It is a stake which means a great deal to the people involved.
I trust therefore that this measure dealing with water conservation will meet with the wholehearted approval of all hon. members. I trust parliament will recognize the importance and magnitude, and the necessity for enlarging the terms of reference so as to include forest and soil conservation as well, and that this measure may be merely the beginning of a new era that will recognize these basic and essential facts, that our very existence depends upon the maintenance of an adequate supply of these God-given resources which we, in our time, must conserve and which we in our time must not destroy.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join with the others who have already spoken in this debate, and to commend the minister upon having introduced this legislation. On other occasions I have had something to say about the conservation of resources, and at this time I want to emphasize some of the points that I think are fundamental and important.
I believe it was Mark Twain who is credited with having said that a lot of people talk about the weather, but nobody does a great

deal about it. I think that is true of conservation. There has been considerable talk about it, but there has not been a great deal done. I hope this is the beginning of a program that will have long and far-reaching effects.
Hon. members will know that the paint and varnish industry have a slogan that says: Save the surface and you save all. I think that might well be applied to our conservation program, because if the top six inches of soil are lost we will find ourselves in a desperate situation, indeed. Our food supplies would diminish very rapidly.
In connection with the program being undertaken it is most essential that effective co-ordination among federal, provincial and municipal governments be brought about. I want to point out right here that in 1939 the municipalities were collecting 30 cents from the tax dollar, while today they collect only 10 cents. The owners of real property, both in the city and in the country, are finding themselves taxed beyond capacity. We realize, too, that these very people who own real property are the backbone of the country. They are the producers, the labourers and the workmen. So that no longer can the burden be placed entirely upon the municipalities.
It is commendable that the federal government is going to co-operate with provincial governments to the extent of 37J per cent each of the cost of these projects. It was only yesterday that we heard a good deal about the difficulties in connection with the South Saskatchewan river project, and the dam proposed in that area. While these dams are spectacular, so far as Ontario is concerned they are not fundamental to a water conservation project. The place to save water is where it falls.
Water is also a forest problem. In old Ontario it is estimated that about 9 per cent of the land is now covered with forest. In other words 91 per cent of the forest has been removed. Those who have given some study to the subject are of the opinion that in Ontario at least 15 per cent of the area should be forested. I think we should go further than that and say that on an average 20 per cent of the area in old Ontario might well be put back to forest.
One of the counties in southwestern Ontario has its forest coverage reduced to 3 per cent, and the problem of water supply for cities and towns, as well as in farm wells, is becoming very acute in those areas. If we continue at the present rate in the Canadian west I am told, by those who know the subject, that 100 years from now we will have 6,000 square miles of desert. The area is expanding instead of decreasing in spite
Water Resources
of the efforts of P.F.R.A. and other agencies which are at work there. Today all over the world we hear of food shortages and populations increasing at a fast rate, yet not another acre of workable land is being added.
There is another problem to be considered in connection with land taken out of cultivation and put into forests. The immediate municipality will lose a certain amount of taxes. Also this marginal land may be producing small amounts of food of one kind and another and the farmer whose land is taken out of production will find his income reduced. Care must be exercised in the administration of this to provide income to take the place of that derived from land taken out of agricultural production.
We hear a great deal today about deficiency diseases because of a lack of certain elements in our food. This should be part of any conservation program. In many areas certain elements are missing from the land and they have not been replaced. Consequently we are faced with this problem of deficiency diseases, not only in connection with humans but in connection with animals as well. One of the statesmen of the United States once said: Show me an eroded soil and I will show you an eroded people. That is true today in some parts of the United States.
The minister and many hon. members have received copies of a brief from the agricultural institute of Canada which contains a well-thought-out program which might well be considered. They point out that there is a possibility of overlapping in government departments which would add to the cost but which would add nothing to the net result. We must avoid that at all costs, as the cost of government is far too high as it is.
At some time or other nearly every agricultural paper in the United States has referred to the fact that some of the great dams which have been built in that country are faced with the problem of silting. Many times they just try to find a solution for that problem by building another dam. I am going to suggest to the minister that one of the valleys in old Ontario be brought under this legislation and used as an experiment to demonstrate the good results that can be obtained from conservation practices rather than the building of dams.
Twenty per cent of the area should be forested. Contour farming should be practised when the land lends itself to that type of land use. Steep hillsides should be grassed so that heavy rainfall will not wash the soil into the valleys and rivers. Good farm management should be practised. In order to get good results these practices should be

Water Resources
pinpointed on individual farms because a practice that will work on one farm may not work on another a short distance away. No over-all practice can be adopted as a rule of thumb to follow. If all this is linked up with the work being done by the Department of Agriculture, the results should be good.
The construction of farm ponds is good and this practice should be encouraged. I should like to see all this done just as an experiment. I believe this experiment is being made on the Brandywine river near Wilmington, Delaware, in the United States and more information could be obtained on what is happening there from the Country Gentleman of February 1953.
While I am on the subject of conservation I should like to point out that the soils committee of the Middlesex crop improvement association in my own county are carrying out a very worth-while work in connection with individual farms scattered throughout the county. They are demonstrating how soil can be conserved. A good deal of credit is due to the chairman of that committee, Mr. John A. Stewart, and his agricultural assistant, Mr. Ken Pretty. As I say, they are doing a most worth-while work.
People in Ontario welcome this because they realize that money is being raised in the central provinces by means of federal taxes to be spent elsewhere in Canada. They realize that under this legislation at least a certain portion will be spent in the provinces where the money is raised.
It is most essential that good public relations be maintained between the various departments and the farming people. Farmers resent governments at any level coming in and taking their land for any purpose. It is most important that there be good publicity and good public relations maintained if this policy is going to be worked out to the satisfaction of all concerned. We have in my county the Fanshawe dam part of the Thames valley authority program. There is bound to be some dissatisfaction. As far as it is humanly possible the people who own the land should be dealt with rather than to have some construction company come along and say, "We have nothing to do with it, just talk to somebody else." That sort of thing leaves a wrong impression.
The farm people should be assured that, if they enter into some long-term plan to reforest their lands, they will remain in ownership of those lands. We hear a lot today about the state taking over the ownership of all means of production. I point that out because the party to my left apparently think and believe that is the way we should

go; but I am unalterably opposed. How can you have incentive to improve and bring into being these conservation practices, which will return their profits to the farmer over a long period of years, if they say: Oh, well, twenty years from now the state is going to take over the whole blessed business so why should I worry about it or why should my children worry about it? There must be some knowledge, on the part of the people who are going to be affected, that they will own the land for a long period of time.
After all, conservation Is really what the Conservative party stands for not only in politics and economics, but in agriculture as well. To point out a few of the thoughts of other people on this matter I have before me some clippings from various publications of one kind and another. I am not going to use a lot of the material but I will take a paragraph here and there from some of them. The first one is from a Royal Bank letter of February, 1949:
In old Ontario, according to the report of the royal commission on forestry, 1947, forest cover has shrunk to 9-7 per cent. Groups which have studied the question estimate that up to 8.000 square miles, or 5,120,000 acres, of waste land should be returned to forests; the commission itself is convinced that at least two and a half million acres of old Ontario might profitably be reforested.
Another extract I have reads:
Erosion, the washing and blowing away of topsoil still goes on. Poor land management and poor forestry practices are pouring wealth down the drain. Our rivers are choked with silt and soil.
The world is spotted with cemeteries of agricultural neglect. There is Greece, once the world's cultural and military leader. Twenty centuries have passed, and today Greece is reduced to a barren nation. Only two per cent of her original topsoil is left. Once, six out of every ten acres were forestland; today one out of twenty is forest. Centuries of cutting and burning, careless farming and overgrazing have reduced this country to an importer nation. The land cannot support her people; Greece imports half of its bread, three-fourths of its rice. Greece slipped from the throne of nations in near pace with the slipping away of her productive lands.
It is estimated that it takes anywhere from 300 to 1,000 years to produce one inch of topsoil. The Toronto Globe and Mail of December 19, 1952, comments on the throne speech as follows:
There is a good deal of merit in this point. Soil, water and forest conservation are almost inseparable. If there is to be conservation at all, it must of necessity integrate all three phases. Agriculture depends on soil and water, and both of these derive protection from woodland. There can be large and spectacular dams, but no conservation of soil or water where it is needed.
And further on:
But what is important in their protest is that the new program be not confined to building big

dams. Unless there is grass roots soil conservation, too, these dams will become mere monuments to folly.
My next quotation is also from a Royal Bank letter, dated August, 1946:
In one small area in Ontario there are 75 farm buildings classed as fair or poor, while 44 buildings have been abandoned or levelled, every one an unwritten story of hope, toil and disappointment. In some cases the land was good to start with, but it was farmed without foresight. The plow made it ready for carrying away by wind and water. Productivity declined. Income decreased. Sons and daughters went away to cities. A farm which housed, fed and clothed a big family only a few years ago supports no one, and is a menace to its neighbours. Once it deposited money in banks, bought machinery, was the mainstay of local retail business and a customer of the mail order houses. It helped feed cities. Today it buys nothing, pays no taxes, produces nothing to add to the national income or the welfare of the country, feeds no one.
Look westward. In 1941 there were more than 4 million acres of abandoned farms in the prairie provinces, an acreage which, at the long time average yield of 15-6 bushels per acre, might produce 62,400,000 bushels of wheat a year if the land had been saved.
The London Free Press on January 15, 1953, also commenting on this resolution, states:
Canada is embarked on a vast program for the development of her natural resources. The picture is bright and attractive. It could easily become dark and disastrous. Now is the time to set about the provision of adequate protective measures for all our natural resources. A long-term conservation policy covering the whole of the dominion is needed.
Now, gentlemen, I want to support the resolution and I hope the minister will take into consideration the many factors that will come before him, and that we will proceed with this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak for a moment or two in support of this resolution and to commend the minister and his department for the work that has already been done.
In the section of the country which I represent we have possibly the most famous of these conservation schemes. Situated on the edge of my riding we have the Shand dam. This is a three-purpose dam built first as a flood control measure to protect the cities of Galt, London and Brantford, and as a means of conservation because the area surrounding the huge pond that is created by this dam has been almost completely reforested. It supplies water during the summer months to flush out the river and thus greatly assists in the disposal of sewage from those cities which I have mentioned. That dam has worked with the greatest of success. It was so successful that a second dam known as the Luther dam, has been built farther up the Grand river.
Water Resources
This is a different situation than the Shand dam which held back the water in a deep pond in a comparatively small area. The dam that has been constructed on the Luther marsh has at no place a depth of over ten or fifteen feet and I imagine that the average depth would perhaps be three or four feet. Peat bog is the principal soil flooded, and last spring the vegetation began to grow through and out of the water. To look at it you would hardly know that it actually was a pond. This dam was supposed to assist in flushing out the river to the extent of about one-quarter of the effect achieved by the Shand dam. Because of the tremendous area that was exposed to the sun, evaporation took place and most of the water stored in that pond evaporated. The farmers in that district felt that this was the best thing that could have happened, because instead of having hot dry winds blowing over their farms during the summer and drying out their crops they had a moist breeze which encouraged growth on the surrounding farms to a great extent. This is easily understood when we realize that a single deciduous apple tree will give off some tons of water during a hot summer day. Thus it is easy to see that, if we encourage reforestation and the ponding of water, we are going to put tons of moisture into the air which covers the farms; otherwise this moisture would not be there. Through a study of history and geography one can see that deserts have occurred in the areas where the trees have been cut. Knowing the huge quantities of water put into the air by each tree, one can understand why these hot dry winds which result from the cutting down of trees cause desert areas. From the experience we have had at the Luther dam, far different from the experience we had with the Shand dam, we believe that it is a better type of dam and far more useful to the country than the deep Shand dam which was built some twelve years ago.
With this in mind I would recommend to the minister that a great deal more thought be given to encouraging farmers to create ponds of three or four acres in low-lying swampy places on their farms. They should be encouraged to grow trees around these ponds which will distribute the moisture into the air, thus cooling the air and encouraging the crops growing in the surrounding fields. Everyone who has flown in an airplane knows the difference in the air over a forested area as compared with the air over ordinary farm fields. In this country we have to take the necessary steps to see that we have more forests in our farm areas. I am pleased to note that the minister has seen fit to set up an item in his estimates to start the Conestogo

Water Resources
dam. I wish to commend him for that. With these three dams in the relatively small area with which I am connected, I think we will have set an example to many other sections of the dominion, and I would invite representatives from all parts of Canada to come and see what has been done by industrious people in that area of this province who have encouraged reforestation and the retention of our natural resources.

I wish to say a very few words concerning this resolution brought forward by the minister, Mr. Speaker. It might be my only opportunity of supporting it. It is a wonderful thing when a minister of the crown introduces a resolution of this kind urging the provinces to take assistance from the federal government for the development and conservation of certain resources. When I listened to this debate at first, I was inclined to believe that the resolution concerned only western Canada because the central theme of the debate was water conservation for that great province in the west which seems to be perishing from the lack of water. However, I was glad to see the interest taken in this subject by the maritime provinces as well as the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
In my opinion this resolution is just the forerunner of a policy which should be introduced by the government, namely, a policy not only for the development and conservation of water resources but for the development of all our natural resources. As some speakers have said during this debate, we have natural resources that are the greatest of any country in the world, yet we have no direct policy from this government for the encouragement and development of those natural resources.
I am going to deal briefly with water conservation for Prince Edward Island. We have no great rivers or great bays in that province. However, we are different from most of the provinces in that we are entirely surrounded by water. Some years ago our province produced wheat, but then western Canada was able to produce the wheat and put flour into the province at a lower price than we could produce it. During the time we were producing wheat, there were many mill ponds and mill dams scattered throughout the length and breadth of the province to operate the various grinding mills. Today these ponds and dams have practically disappeared. There are only a few operating. The provincial government, in co-operation with the fisheries department, has been rebuilding some of these dams and conserving the water in these ponds. I want to bring this to the

attention of the minister, because so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned I believe he should seriously consider the restoration of these mill ponds and mill dams, in co-operation with the fisheries department, for fish culture. I might say that this would be one of the best things that could be done, especially in the interest of the tourist trade.
Several of these ponds have already been rebuilt, but some of them have not been built in a manner that would make them useful to the fisheries department for fish culture. I know there are a great many other members who wish to speak on this resolution. As I said at the beginning that I was only to draw one matter to the attention of the minister, namely, the restoration of the mill ponds throughout our province, I shall close by telling him that if he will co-operate with the fisheries department in putting these mill ponds into use as fish culture ponds it will be of great benefit to the province. They will be an asset by giving sport fishing to many of the tourists who visit the island.
Again I say I have great pleasure in supporting this resolution. I hope that the minister will come to see us with reference to securing better conservation and rebuilding our mill ponds.

Mr. Speaker, I just wish to say a few words in support of this resolution. The Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) is in the happy position, I think, that he has introduced a measure which has the support of every member in this house, and deservedly so; because in my opinion there is in Canada today no question that is more important than is conservation. Our future as a nation depends on it. Over the years we have listened to enthusiastic propagandists in this country who told us that our resources were inexhaustible and all that kind of thing. The fact is that they are not inexhaustible. Not only have we been using them but we have been wasting them at such a rate that, if we are going to conserve and to keep ahead of the wastage, it will be necessary that a great deal of money be spent.
There has come to my notice recently a book entitled "Conservation in Canada" by Professor O. M. McConkey of the Ontario Agricultural College at Guelph. I would recommend this book for reading to the members of this house. A moment ago I used a certain phrase and perhaps I unconsciously had it in mind from reading the book. At page 12 of his book Professor McConkey says:
Our future as a nation depends on a national plan of soil building and conservation to which all governments, rural and urban interests, and each

citizen of Canada can work. We have before us the example of the United States where action has been taken; the U.S. soil conservation service, started in 1933, has developed over two thousand conservation districts covering 80 per cent of all the farms in the U.S.A. This service co-operates with farmers and brings a land use and conservation plan to each farm. But it was too late-
That is, too late to prevent the great harm that had been done. To continue:
-it is estimated that over one hundred million acres of farm land had been destroyed before action was taken.
Perhaps the damage has not occurred on that scale in Canada, but there has been a terrific waste of farmland in this country. On the next page of his book the professor says:
Here in North America the exploitation of our natural resources has been savage and rapid. Within an incredibly short time-from one to three hundred years in the east and seventy-five years on the western prairies-we have destroyed more than a hundred million acres of fertile soil.
If we are going to undo the harm that has been done we shall, as I say, have to spend a great deal of money. I think the minister can get that money provided he makes the necessary effort to inform the people of this country. I believe they are now ready to listen to him or to anyone else who will give them the true story of the misuse we have made of our natural resources. If congratulations are in order for bringing in this resolution as a start, I freely give them to the minister. I hope he will lose no time in seeking the co-operation of the provinces to develop in Canada a conservation program that will be really worth while.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I want to speak about this range of land mass between Ottawa and west of lake Simcoe in the province of Ontario. In my opinion there are in this resolution three things that cannot be separated, namely the conservation of our water, the conservation of our land and the conservation of our forests. Each one of them is so dependent on the other that one cannot exist alone without the use of the other.
This range of land area across this country has been a great watershed. It is a great reservoir for such things as the Rideau canal, the Trent canal and the great lakes in the province of Ontario. The height of land divides the northern section of the county of Haliburton; there the height of land is reached in southern Ontario, and the water runs west towards lake Simcoe and Georgian bay, and north into the Ottawa river, and south to lake Ontario, the waters of the great lakes and St. Lawrence river. This area has become a great reservoir. Great
Water Resources
concrete dams have been built practically all over this whole area for the conservation of water.
I am glad that the minister has made it possible that what is done will be in co-operation with the province; because in this great area, as to the way the water is controlled now, it is in co-operation with the province. The water is controlled not only for the canals but also for the Ontario hydro.
As to this great range of lakes, there is an area of sixty-six feet around all the commercial lakes, you might say, or the larger ones. That sixty-six feet is mentioned in some agreement made probably one hundred years ago between the province and the Dominion of Canada, or at least probably at the time of confederation. That was more or less called the road allowance although it is never used for that purpose. It is used for the control of water. In other words, when you put in a dam you can raise the water sixty-six feet back on to the land without paying anybody anything. At the same time the land and the timber on the sixty-six feet is owned by the people or the company or whoever it might be that own the land back behind it.
I think that is something that should be adjusted. Some arrangements should be made between the province and the Dominion of Canada to the effect that, where a dam has been put in, this sixty-six feet should no longer exist; because over the years, as they put in a dam, in many places this sixty-six feet is already covered when the water it at high level. Therefore the high-water mark should not measure from the outside edge of this sixty-six feet from the lake but should measure from where the original surveys were taken at low-water level.
On a hot humid day water disappears rather fast. On one of our hottest days in the summer two inches of water will be taken off one of these big lakes by the process of evaporation. Something must be done to bring that water from the soil and from the great watershed back into the lake. Nature takes it up and brings it down in rain, but it does not always come back into the lake; it goes back onto the great range of the watershed.
There is another feature about this resolution that I like. The dominion government has seen fit to step into the picture and to do something about it in co-operation with the provinces. To conserve this water you must do something before it gets into the river. You must conserve it in the lake, in the little stream, in the ponds that are spread out throughout the length and breadth of this land. As I said before, great dams

Water Resources
have been built, but that is not enough. What happens in the spring every year after our timber has gone or a fire has ravaged the area is that with the first hot sun in March away goes the snow. It is down in the lake in a day or two. Your lake is filled to the top of the dam. The inspectors must open the stop logs, and let that water go down the river, so that the great waste of water takes place in the spring of the year in places where we have not timber conservation and where we have no fire reservoir. It is high time that this problem was solved.
The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) gave us an illustration of the value of water. He told us how water is used in mining, in industry and in every aspect of our life in this country. If this great area was reforested it would be to the great advantage of us all. The province of Ontario has done considerable work along that line. They have great tree plantations from which any land owner or anybody else who wants to plant trees may obtain them. That system did not work out too successfully because many people obtained trees but did not plant them properly, and great waste was made of them. Now when you obtain trees you must pay a cent each for them. I myself plant 8,000 or 10,000 trees every year. I endeavour to plant as many trees as will in thirty-five years amount to as much timber as I cut, or even more, in a year. This system has been carried on by a considerable number of lumbermen on more or less privately-owned lands. It should be carried on to an even greater extent by this resolution.
The time has come when the government should be doing something along the line of producing trees and cover on these great watersheds and thereby preserve the water so that the cover will hold the snow and the ice in the bush in the spring of the year. I have seen swamps, low places in the timber, which have had ice in the bottom of them, some of it probably under a foot of topsoil, in the month of June. If our country was properly handled that would take place all over the high land mass. We would not have the run-off in the spring; we would not have our wasted water in the spring. We would have that water going into our lakes, creeks and rivers gradually until around the first of July. That is when your dams would come into use to make your reservoirs in the lakes.
Some arrangement should be arrived at between the dominion and the provinces with regard to the trapping of beaver. At one time in our country in this great range we had little beaver meadows a mile long

or two miles long which would have four or five feet of water in them. Through our arrangement for trapping beaver, many miles of this area have been trapped out and the last beaver has gone and the dams are rotted out. The beaver meadow, instead of being full of water, has turned out to be a fire hazard in the summertime because it is full of dead grass.
Those ponds full of water served a useful purpose in fire protection because the fire rangers that the province has at the present time could go in there with their hoses and little pumps and that sort of thing and they could get water to put out the fires.
This resolution should go further than it does for this reason. In the Financial Post of five or six months ago this article appeared. They were commenting on the sixth British commonwealth forestry conference which was held here during the past summer, and this is what it says:
This country doesn't know whether we're cutting down trees too last. Of eighteen countries represented at the sixth British commonwealth forestry conference now in progress here, Canada and British Guiana alone are unable to give any estimate of the extent to which new forest growth is matching annual utilization and other depletion of forest resources.
In contrast are the precise and complete set of figures furnished by Great Britain which shows that new growth in 1950 was 130*9 million cubic feet against total depletion of 100*2 m.c.f. In Canada it will be at least three years before even a partial answer can be obtained to the question of whether our forests can continue in perpetuity producing at today's rate. By that time there should be a completed forest inventory in at least eight of the ten provinces.
Canada's report to the conference says it seems probable that considerable proportions of the Canadian forest are being cut too heavily, and adds that there is "urgent" need for more intensive sustained yield forest management.
Meanwhile Canada is taking an annual harvest from her forests that in volume is 50 per cent greater than the collective output of all other commonwealth countries. Over-all Canadian forest output in 1950 was 3,322 m.c.f. Output for the rest of the commonwealth was 2,260 m.c.f. with the largest part of it produced in India, Australia and Uganda.
It was not to our government's credit that they did not have any figures to show the conference with respect to what has been done along this line.
The Ontario conservation association held a meeting in the Normal school in Ottawa a few days ago, and I find this report in the Ottawa Journal:
Federal and provincial governments should assist the townships to control bush fires in the settled townships of Ontario, the executive of zone five, Ontario Conservation Association, decided yesterday at a meeting in the Normal school, Ottawa. Major Angus McDonald, of Alexandria, wui chairman for the meeting.
The reeves believe that some system, corresponding to that which has been develope-J in the

United States, since passage of the Weekes' Act, in 1911, would fit the needs of the rural municipalities.
At the present time there are no provincial employees authorized to take any part in fire fighting, outside of the fire district in northern Ontario, which is protected by the provincial service.
That is something that should be done. There should be more fire protection for this great range of land, and it should be reforested. I have other clippings that I could read but they are practically all the same. I am glad that the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) has seen fit to bring in this resolution. I am also pleased that he has said that this work will be carried on in co-operation with the provinces, because the provinces control the cutting of our timber. That is true of Ontario, at least. We know that the provinces control a certain amount of water conservation, and that they work in conjunction with the dominion government with respect to the use of the canals, and so on; whereas the water in all this great area is controlled by the dominion government. The inspectors are paid by the dominion government. They are the men who put in the logs in the spring and take them out gradually during the summer months to let the water down at a gradual flow. As I said before, this resolution does not go far enough. We have to do something to reforest this great watershed so that it will hold back the snow, ice and moisture in the spring of the year, and not let it away with the first signs of spring.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

I do not know what the bill will contain and perhaps the minister will want to leave this until the bill comes down, but I wonder if there cannot be some sort of synchronization with water conservation so that these floods can be controlled. When the Fraser river flooded a few years ago it was regarded as a national catastrophe. When a small town
Water Resources
is flooded it is not considered a national catastrophe, but the results are just as serious to the people in that town as to people in larger centres. It is only a matter of number, for the consequences to the individual businessman or home owner are just as serious whether he lives in a small or large community.
A few years ago when one of these towns was flooded I took up the matter with the Minister of Public Works and the dominion government did some flood control work as a relief scheme. At that time they wanted to put men to work so that they could earn their bread and butte*. But when floods occurred later on there were no relief schemes available. Of course there was no money from this government to control any floods there and it was a matter of passing the responsibility from one government to another government, and when they both begin to pass it over from one to another you just cannot get anywhere at all.
So, I would like to know if the minister can give us any information that would be valuable in that respect. Perhaps to make my question a little more direct I might ask him this: Are these various or smaller projects going to be the responsibility of the provincial government after these grants have been given to the provinces? Is it going to be left to their discretion to spend the money the way they wish? Are smaller projects going to be brought into the picture or just the larger ones? If the minister can, I would like him to give the house some information along that line.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to leave the details of the answer until the bill is before the house. I can tell my hon. friend that flood control is one of the main features envisaged by the legislation we are now seeking to introduce.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: The minister has just told us that flood control is one of the principal features of this bill. I wonder if he would mind telling us whether, in devising this scheme, the government had all of the provinces in mind or only those which especially suffered from lack of flood control.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: We had all provinces in mind, Mr. Chairman, and we communicated with all provincial governments.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
There seems to be some fear of overlapping between the Department of Resources and Development and the Department of Agriculture. I wonder if the minister could explain where the dividing line is to be drawn.
This afternoon the hon. member for Kootenay West referred to a brief submitted

Water Resources
by the Agricultural Institute of Canada within recent weeks. I also have a copy of that brief. They are very much concerned because this policy is to be under the Department of Resources and Development. I know that in the province of British Columbia the people are very anxious to have the P.F.R.A., which is under the Department of Agriculture, extended to that province to undertake the various projects. Apparently P.F.R.A. has had considerable success in developing projects and the demand is for them to undertake projects which I believe would be of the type envisaged by this resolution.
Can the minister tell us just where the line is to be drawn? I hope this is not to be another case of building up two kingdoms in the government with overlapping functions. There does seem to be some danger of that happening and perhaps the minister could explain where the dividing line could be drawn.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
It is not intended, of course, that there shall be any overlapping of functions. The approach to the problem has been at all times that the type of work envisaged by this bill is carried out by the water resources division of the department. That division has been in the department ever since it was the department of the interior.
In our dealings with Ontario, that province's operations have been under its department of planning and development. They did not visualize these projects to be of a type that would in any way conflict with their department of agriculture, nor do we in the federal government. There is no intention of having overlapping in the two fields of activity at all. The act under which the Department of Resources and Development was set up makes the two fields of jurisdiction clear and I can assure hon. members that there is no intention to have overlapping.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: One other question. Would this measure enable the Department of Resources and Development to undertake work in connection with such a project as the conservation of water in the Columbia river basin? As the minister knows, the Americans have used that river to almost the maximum possible extent, I take it, in so far as the river is in their territory, but in Canada there is some division of authority between the dominion and the province. I am wondering if the development of the Columbia river basin would come under this measure. I know that the minister's department has for some years been making investigations and surveys and giving help of that kind in the Columbia river basin, but will the whole project come under this measure or could it come under this measure?

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: It is difficult to answer that question until we know what the whole project will be. At present there is a survey on the Columbia river basin being carried out under the general jurisdiction of the international joint commission. Certain responsibilities have been assigned to the Canadian section of that commission to conduct surveys; and the water resources division of the Department of Resources and Development has assumed the general responsibility for making the surveys and collecting the data. Once the surveys have been completed and the data compiled it will then be possible to see what the development of the basin should be; but up to that time, not knowing what program of works will commend itself, it is difficult to say who should carry it out.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Would the development of the basin come under the international joint commission or would it be under either the federal or the provincial government? Surely the international joint commission would not actually do the development work. I can understand why they are making the surveys or directing the surveys but they would not have jurisdiction over the actual development.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: The hon. member is correct in that.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Is there any authority which would have the direction of the actual development?

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: The question of the actual development would be largely for the provinces. The resources are within the jurisdiction of the provinces and they have the prime responsibility for their development. It is entirely possible that there will be a private enterprise approach to any development that takes place in that basin, and if it takes place it will be with the full knowledge, consent and under the jurisdiction of the provincial government.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Would the dominion government not have anything to do with the development? Mind you, the river system is navigable, so the Department of Public Works would have some responsibility. Would the dominion government not come into that picture at all?

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
I am quite sure there would be consultation and each government would work within its own sphere of influence. The development of water resources is, in the first instance, under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. This is a basin which has potentialities of great magnitude and I

have no doubt that if it is to be developed to the fullest extent there will be co-operation between all levels of government.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on the Burnt river at Kinmount, Ontario, there has been a dam built. I do not know how long ago it was built but it was there long before I was there. It is a timber dam, its piers filled with stone. The piers have become very rotten and the dam is apt to go out at any time. I have been after the Department of Transport, and through them the Minister of Public Works, to rebuild that dam but they have refused to do so until now. A small village of 250 people could arrange to put up $5,000 but that is as far as they could possibly go. I believe the province is likely to come in on it from the tourist angle. Would the federal government be in a position to grant money for 37 J per cent of the cost of that project?

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext: I cannot say. I am not familiar with the project. I would have to see it and study it.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES FOR CONSERVATION PURPOSES
speechtext:
We will make you familiar
with it.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to provide for the establishment of the historic sites and monuments board of Canada on a statutory basis; to provide that the board shall consist of twelve members and for its powers and duties; to provide also that the appointed members shall be paid a fee for attending each meeting and travelling and living expenses incurred in connection with the business of the board; to provide also for the appointment and remuneration of a secretary of the board; and to provide further that all expenditures for the purposes of the act shall be paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament therefor.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext: Could we have a statement from the minister now as to the necessity for this legislation?

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext:
Since the motion is one for the Speaker to leave the chair, and since we have gone through this debate on a
Historic Sites and Monuments number of occasions, I think it would be preferable if the statement were made after we are in the committee of the whole, at which time I shall be pleased to make brief remarks.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall, Mr. Chairman, that the historic sites and monuments board was set up by the governor in council in 1919 for the purpose of advising the government in the selection and commemoration of sites and events of national historic importance. With the exception of changes in personnel from time to time, the board has functioned on this more or less informal basis up to the present. Its terms of reference have never been clearly or formally defined.
The bill referred to in the resolution proposes to establish the board on a statutory basis and to define its duties and powers. It is proposed that the board shall be composed of twelve members; ten to be appointed by the governor in council and to represent each of the provinces. The other two members would be the dominion archivist and chief curator of the national museum. Provision is being sought to authorize payment to the appointed members of a fee for attending each meeting and for the payment to all the members of travelling and living expenses incurred by them in connection with the work of the board. Authority is also being sought for the appointment and remuneration of a secretary of the board. The bill will also ask for authority to establish historic museums and to acquire land for such purpose. -
I do not think there is anything further I need say at this time. I am sure that all hon. members will agree with the desirability of establishing the board on a more permanent basis, thus giving greater recognition to the importance of the work it will be asked to perform in the years to come.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext:
I believe all hon. members will agree with the minister that we establish this board on a permanent basis. Recently I had the honour of representing the minister at the unveiling of a tablet to commemorate one of the outstanding Canadians of a few years ago. I had the opportunity also of attending with the Prime Minister when, under the direction of this historic sites and monuments board of Canada, there was unveiled in the city of Belleville a memorial to the late Sir Mackenzie Bowell, who was prime minister of Canada from December 21, 1894, until

Historic Sites and Monuments April 27, 1896. Sir Mackenzie Bowell represented the old constituency of Hastings North.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS

I realize the interest that the hon. member has in all the monuments that he has seen unveiled, but on the other hand I am afraid if I allow him to carry on I shall be opening a door which certainly will not be closed this evening. Therefore, I would ask him not to discuss any matter but that which is relevant to the resolution.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext: I was only endeavouring to point out to the committee the work that this group of ten representatives, one from each province, has attempted to do and has been doing. I believe that the group has been doing great work and, as the minister says in his resolution, apparently without any remuneration. I believe that a board so important as this particular board should be recognized in legislation, and should be properly compensated for the work it has done and is doing. I am sure that all members of the committee will join with the minister in supporting the legislation that he introduces.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext: It was fitting that today the government should announce that they would erect a monument on parliament hill to one of the Conservative prime ministers, and that the hon. member for Hastings South should be allowed to refer to another distinguished Conservative prime minister to whom another monument has been erected in Belleville.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext: It must be a good wicket.

I notice that the minister has not followed the recommendation of the royal commission on arts and sciences. It was not, of course, necessary that he should do so. The royal commission recommended that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec should have two representatives each, and also that the Canadian historical association should have the privilege of nominating two of its members for five years. The recommendation has not been followed, but other recommendations seem to have been followed in the main.
Now, sir, I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to references which have been made in the report of the royal commission to this very important subject. They are found in two sections, part I, chapter 11, and also in part II at page 346. If I may, sir, I should like to draw the attention of the committee to a reference which is contained therein to the province of rMr. Follwell.]
Newfoundland. The reference is found at page 129 of the report and reads as follows:
An area rich in historic sites as old and even older than any in the rest of Canada is Newfoundland. We heard of nearly sixty sites of general historic interest awaiting the attention of the historic sites and monuments board. We were told of the traditional landing place of John Cabot (June 24, 1497), of Carbonear, where the early Channel Island settlers produced the "charbon" for heating their homes, of old graves of Basque fishermen, and of the site of Lord Baltimore's castle inhabited by David Kirke and others.
David Kirke is the Sir David Kirke who conquered Quebec when Champlain was first there.
We were taken back not to the eighteenth century but to the seventeenth and (for a brief moment) to the fifteenth. Canada's newest province proudly and rightly claims her place beside the oldest.
There is no doubt that this board has a great deal of work to do which perhaps could not be easily done by a voluntary organization.
